candidateRows: Religious metaphysical claims are false explanations inherited from humanity's fearful and scientifically ignorant infancy.
This directly supports the anti-theist side by denying religion's foundational truth claims and offering a naturalistic account of their origin.
At the outset of his opening case, Hitchens contrasts ancient supernatural explanations with later scientific knowledge and denies that any creator has been demonstrated.
Claims to know God's wishes confer unjustified authority on religious speakers and reveal religion as a human design for power.
It connects unverifiable divine knowledge to prescriptive control, supplying a central mechanism for the claim that religion is harmful and man-made.
Hitchens moves from the inability to prove a designer to the greater claim that clergy purport to know divine preferences governing food, sex, and permissible study.
Religion converts alleged divine authority into dictatorial temporal power, with theocracy illustrating its capacity for extreme cruelty.
The move supplies a concrete causal account of religious poisoning: insulated divine warrants empower coercive institutions and remove ordinary challenges to authority.
Hitchens argues that religious officials seek power in the present world, then uses theocratic Iran to illustrate conduct enabled by belief in divine authorization.
A personally supervising creator would impose total surveillance, compulsory submission, and potentially eternal punishment, making theism itself undesirable.
The argument attacks not merely the evidence for God but the moral desirability of the religious proposition at the heart of the debate.
Hitchens distinguishes atheism from anti-theism and portrays divine supervision, heavenly servility, and eternal torture as the ultimate totalitarian abolition of individuality.
The proliferation and violent conflict of incompatible religions are best explained by humans creating gods rather than God creating humanity.
This provides an affirmative explanatory argument for religion's human origin while tying sectarian plurality to recurring intolerance and violence.
Hitchens contrasts two origin hypotheses, argues that human invention explains religious multiplicity, and cites sectarian destruction in Iraq and the Balkans.
American liberty depends on separation of religion and state, including freedom from religion, and citizens should resist religious imposition.
The move turns his critique into a civic consequence, arguing that constitutional safeguards are necessary because competing faiths seek coercive public authority.
Hitchens praises the American constitutional separation of church and state, recalls sectarian threats to religious liberty, and warns against religious control of law and education.
Acknowledging religious wrongdoing does not establish the sweeping claim that religion poisons everything, because the charge requires excluding substantial good.
This directly contests the debate's sweeping anti-religious thesis by attacking its universal scope and placing the burden on the absolute term in the charge.
Hitchens's overarching contention that religion is false, harmful, and poisonous in all of its manifestations.
Olasky concedes that religious motivation has produced serious harms but argues that even a modest proportion of religious good defeats an unqualified universal indictment.
Religious traditions have produced independent-minded believers, inspiring public leadership, and cooperation among different faiths rather than mere servility and intolerance.
The examples directly rebut several mechanisms in the anti-theist case by presenting religious inspiration, argument with God, and interfaith coexistence.
Hitchens's claims that religion produces servility, has ceased to inspire, and cannot tolerate coexistence among faiths.
Olasky invokes biblical figures who argued with God, religiously inflected leadership against injustice and communism, and cooperative action by multiple faith communities.
Confident dismissal of biblical history is unwarranted because sustained scholarship and archaeological discoveries have supported accounts once labeled mythical.
Historical credibility is a principal defense of Christianity against the allegation that its foundational narratives are simply false human fabrications.
Hitchens's categorical dismissal of Exodus, Mosaic traditions, and ancient religious thinkers as fictional products of human infancy.
Olasky challenges categorical claims about Mosaic fiction by noting archaeological confirmation of previously doubted peoples and rulers and the work of learned ancient-language scholars.
Christian belief motivates costly care for vulnerable children and overseas orphans, contradicting the claim that evangelism is wholly fraudulent or poisonous.
The extended counterexample directly addresses whether religion poisons everything by identifying demanding charitable conduct attributed to Christian conviction.
Hitchens's characterization of American evangelism as a heartless racket and religion as poisoning every aspect of life.
Olasky describes church families adopting children with severe needs and congregants prioritizing African orphanages over their own comfort, attributing these sacrifices to Christianity.
Christian conversion and ministry can transform addicts and endangered young people rather than poison their lives.
Concrete cases of rehabilitation and service directly challenge the motion's universal claim that religion poisons everything.
Hitchens's claim that religion poisons everything without meaningful beneficial exceptions.
Olasky moves from a local ministry example to several American programs whose Christian workers rehabilitate addicts, teenagers, refugees, and disabled people.
Christian convictions materially contributed to American charity, divided government, and freedom of the press.
The argument attributes major humanitarian and civic institutions to Christianity, providing a broad historical rebuttal to the motion.
Hitchens's contention that religion is poisonous and deserves no credit for humane or civic achievements.
Olasky cites nineteenth-century relief work, Christian ideas behind dispersed political power, and the Zenger trial as beneficial historical consequences of belief.
Research on missions, literacy, hospitals, and modern activism supports a mixed rather than wholly poisonous account of Christianity.
The move directly contests the universal wording of the motion through scholarly claims and contemporary examples of Christian social benefit.
Hitchens's universal characterization of religion as poisoning everything despite evidence of beneficial activism.
Olasky invokes scholarship connecting Protestant missions with education and literacy, then cites evangelical campaigns against trafficking, slavery, and prison rape.
Religious charity does not validate religion because humane work needs no supernatural motive and religious identity can equally accompany atrocity.
The distinction between charity and religious truth directly answers the principal con argument and preserves the anti-theist case despite benevolent believers.
Olasky's claim that Christian charitable works refute the proposition that religion poisons everything.
Hitchens contrasts Joseph Kony's explicitly Christian violence with Christian rehabilitation workers, arguing that secular people can perform the same humane work without added doctrine.
Religiously motivated social service is not evidence for a faith because it may seek converts or rewards and is practiced by harmful sectarian movements too.
The move supplies a general reason why benevolent institutions cannot establish religious truth or excuse destructive religious organizations.
Olasky's reliance on Christian service providers and charitable institutions as proof against the anti-religion case.
Hitchens questions ulterior religious incentives, compares Christian charity with Hamas and Hezbollah social services, and argues that orphanages reveal nothing about a religion's merits.
Martin Luther King used a humane metaphor rather than the violent biblical Exodus, whose narrative lacks archaeological support.
The argument denies Christianity exclusive credit for civil rights and uses the underlying scripture to challenge both biblical morality and historical credibility.
Olasky's invocation of Martin Luther King and Christian leadership as evidence of religion's beneficial moral force.
Hitchens situates King among secular and leftist allies, distinguishes King's liberation metaphor from biblical conquest, and says archaeology has not verified Exodus.
Human courage and military success should not be credited to supernatural intervention or treated as products of religious virtue.
The move articulates the broader anti-theist principle that attributing human achievements to God degrades human virtue and lacks explanatory force.
Olasky's reported attribution of Washington's victory and military effectiveness to godly policies.
Hitchens credits French intervention and other material factors, invokes irreligious or intemperate military success, and warns against attaching supernatural explanations to courage.
Hitchens's case is weak because it defines religion as wholly evil while excluding religious motives whenever believers do good.
This is a direct logical attack on the universal motion claim, alleging one-sided classification of good and bad religious consequences.
Hitchens's method of denying religious attribution for good works while using religious attribution for harms.
Olasky proposes a mixed accounting of religion's effects, says Hitchens insists on an absolute verdict, and notes that King's coalition included Christians as well as secularists.
Christianity is principally a story of divine creation, human fallenness, rescue, sacrificial love, and promised redemption rather than a mere rulebook.
The move presents the con side's affirmative account of Christianity as grace and redemption, directly addressing the debate's central alternative to poison.
Hitchens's treatment of biblical commands and violent claimants as representative of Christianity's essential content.
Olasky recounts creation, rebellion, evil, covenant, sacrifice, divine persistence, Christ's redemption, and present glimpses of self-sacrificial love despite continuing sin.
The command against the Amalekites should be understood as an exceptional wartime response to an exceptionally dangerous enemy, not ordinary biblical morality.
The move directly answers one of the strongest scriptural-morality objections by framing civilian deaths as a tragic problem of exceptional warfare.
Hitchens's charge that Exodus endorses divinely authorized conquest, killing, enslavement, and seizure of land.
Olasky identifies the Amalekites as an extreme threat, acknowledges the horror of civilian deaths, and compares the dilemma with Allied bombing of German cities.
The extreme improbability of spontaneous life makes divine creation and extraordinary Christian miracles comparatively credible.
It directly answers the charge that foundational Christian claims are incredible by comparing them with the improbability attributed to life's natural origin.
Hitchens's contention that the virgin birth, resurrection, and other foundational Christian claims are incredible.
After defending biblical warfare contextually, Olasky turns to probability, arguing that accepting life's highly improbable emergence weakens objections to creation and miracles.
Evolution is an undirected, pitiless, and contingent process that neither intended humanity nor assigns humanity cosmic importance.
The argument supplies a naturalistic alternative to providential creation and directly contests the claim that improbable life points toward divine purpose.
Olasky's probability argument that life's unlikely origin supports creation and makes Christian miracles credible.
Hitchens responds that extinction and evolutionary contingency reveal no purposeful selection, while an indifferent universe neither planned humanity nor notices its disappearance.
Religion combines humiliating doctrines of inherited guilt with the egotistical assurance that the universe and divine plan center on humanity.
It advances a direct explanation of how religion poisons human self-understanding, attacking both religious abasement and claims of privileged cosmic significance.
Olasky's account of sin, redemption, divine love, and Christ's sacrifice as the source of undeserved grace.

Hitchens argues that inherited guilt destroys self-respect while salvation doctrine compensates with solipsistic cosmic importance, making sacrificial redemption both immoral and psychologically degrading.
Biblical killing of Egyptian firstborn children and the Amalekites cannot be morally excused by analogies to terrorism or wartime necessity.
It directly rebuts the principal contextual defense of scriptural mass killing and challenges the morality of accepting children's destruction for a chosen people's redemption.
Olasky's claim that the Amalekites resembled terrorists and that their destruction was defensible within a larger cosmic war.
Hitchens points to the death of Egypt's firstborn and the eradication of peoples, rejecting the claim that unknown victims can be classified as terrorists to vindicate divine violence.
Religion can make otherwise moral people commit wicked acts by presenting genital mutilation and women's subordination as divinely warranted.
This is a direct affirmative mechanism for the motion: alleged divine authority corrupts ordinary moral instincts and legitimizes bodily harm, misogyny, and degrading conduct.
Using infant circumcision, sexual shame, and religiously sanctioned contempt for women, Hitchens argues that divine permission transforms conduct a moral person would reject into duty.
Calling ordinary honesty a religious duty pollutes its moral integrity and isolated charitable acts cannot establish religion as ethically beneficial.
It directly contests the opposing side's principal evidence of religious benefit by separating autonomous moral action from religious motivation and broader doctrinal consequences.
Olasky's reliance on religious charity, philanthropy, and virtuous conduct as evidence that faith produces moral good.
Hitchens recounts a Muslim driver's honesty but argues the act needs no religious authorization, while one virtuous episode cannot prove Islam or religion morally beneficial overall.
If human existence and thought are wholly random, Hitchens cannot coherently claim certainty or provide reasons to trust his own assertions.
It challenges the epistemic foundation of the naturalistic case by arguing that thoroughgoing randomness undermines confidence in the critic's reasoning and certainty.
Hitchens's account of evolution and human existence as random, unintended, and devoid of providential direction.
Olasky contrasts Hitchens's certainty with his naturalistic account, arguing that thoughts produced by an entirely random reality lack an articulated basis for trust.
The Gospels' prominent female witnesses and precise incidental details count against their being late propaganda and support their historical credibility.
It answers challenges to scriptural reliability with two claimed credibility indicators, supporting the historical foundation on which Christianity's distinctive claims depend.
Hitchens's suggestion that religious scriptures are unbelievable human productions comparable to propaganda rather than credible testimony.

Olasky argues propagandists would not foreground women as resurrection witnesses in that culture and analogizes detailed Gospel reporting to contemporaneous records preserving otherwise forgotten facts.
The mass killing committed by officially atheist regimes shows that poison is not unique to religion and can flourish under secular power.
It directly negates the exclusivity implicit in the motion by using Soviet and Chinese experience to argue that eliminating Christianity does not eliminate oppression or mass violence.
Hitchens's thesis that religion is the distinctive source of pervasive moral corruption, violence, and authoritarian harm.
Olasky invokes the Soviet Union, Maoist China, and their death tolls to argue that secular dictatorships supply a record of poisoning far beyond specifically religious institutions.
Christian grace is an antidote to human poison because forgiveness liberates moral reform, sustained abolitionism, loving relationships, and personal transformation.
It supplies the con side's direct alternative to the motion, distinguishing Christianity from bargaining religion and claiming concrete historical and personal transformation through grace.
Hitchens's overarching assertion that religion poisons everything and that religious morality lacks distinctive ethical value.
Olasky cites Newton and Wilberforce, describes grace as unconditional rather than transactional, and offers his marriage and family history as evidence that Christianity counteracted selfishness.
Christian identity is not equivalent to Republican politics, and religious people across the political spectrum exhibit unusually strong charitable commitment.
The answer directly supports the Christian-grace side by denying partisan exclusivity and presenting charitable conduct as a measurable fruit shared across religious communities.
The audience member's charge that Christianity licenses arrogance, exclusion, and an antagonistic us-versus-them posture.

During audience questions, Olasky distinguishes Christianity from party identity and invokes comparative giving and volunteering to argue that religious commitment unites people across political divisions.
Antitheism differs from mere atheism because divine rule would be undesirable, while the existence of such rule remains unsupported by evidence.
The clarification states both a central normative objection to divine government and the evidential premise underlying Hitchens's anti-theist position.
The questioner's suggestion that Hitchens had substituted personal distaste for an argument that religious claims are false.
Hitchens answers a challenge about whether dislike of doctrine establishes falsity by separating the wish that God not exist from the evidential question of whether God exists.
Religious diversity and apparent natural calamity become intelligible without divine agency, making God an unnecessary explanatory assumption under Occam's razor.
The move advances a broad naturalistic explanation against religion's truth and argues that supernatural hypotheses create mysteries that ordinary causal accounts dissolve.
The questioner's claim that diversity of belief does not itself justify doubting religion and request for a positive case against Christianity.

Hitchens treats human authorship as the simpler explanation for divergent religions, compares theological accounts of disasters with natural explanations, and extends the point to disease and inoculation.
Faith-based resistance to vaccination has helped revive preventable disease, illustrating religion's capacity to obstruct secular humanitarian and medical work.
The contemporary example supplies concrete causal support for the motion and directly counters attempts to credit religion selectively for charitable accomplishments.
The opposing emphasis on religious charity and the questioner's challenge to Hitchens's positive case against religion.
Hitchens describes secular efforts to eradicate polio, religious discouragement of inoculation, renewed disease spread, and the need to count religious harms alongside claimed charitable benefits.
Human morality is innate, socially necessary, and evolutionarily grounded, so basic prohibitions did not originate through supernatural command.
This directly contests the claim that religion grounds morality by supplying a naturalistic origin and arguing that human society presupposed moral knowledge before scripture.
The audience question asking what can ground moral conduct after religious teaching and supernatural authority are removed.
Hitchens grounds morality in human solidarity and evolution, then argues that people necessarily understood murder, theft, and perjury as harmful before receiving biblical commandments.
The Good Samaritan exemplifies non-Christian compassion, while religious law can authorize neglect, showing ordinary humanism to be morally sufficient and sometimes superior.
The move uses a central Christian moral narrative to argue both that compassion precedes Christian teaching and that religious rules can corrupt otherwise humane conduct.
The audience question implying that moral behavior and good works may require religion as their source or sustaining authority.
Hitchens interprets the Samaritan's conduct as spontaneous human solidarity rather than Christian obedience and contrasts it with religious permissions that could prevent aid to an outsider.
Common grace explains morality outside explicit belief, while modern secular society may still depend on inherited moral capital formed by earlier Christian teaching.
The response preserves Christianity's explanatory role despite nonbelievers' morality by invoking common grace and the continuing cultural effects of accumulated Christian formation.
Hitchens's argument that morality is innate, humanism is sufficient, and supernatural authority contributes nothing necessary to ethical conduct.
Olasky answers the secular-morality challenge through common grace and the idea that present society may be drawing on moral understandings developed across prior generations.
Cotton Mather's advocacy of inoculation shows that influential Christian leaders could support medical innovation rather than uniformly obstruct it.
The historical counterexample directly challenges a load-bearing example used to portray religious mentality as inherently hostile to scientific medicine and disease prevention.
Hitchens's use of Timothy Dwight and faith-based vaccine resistance to argue that religion impedes inoculation and medical progress.
Olasky supplements the common-grace answer with the example of Cotton Mather working with Zabdiel Boylston to promote inoculation despite opposition from prominent contemporaries.
The Iraq conflict is partly a struggle against religious parties seeking theocratic barbarism, so defending a secular Iraq is an anti-religious undertaking.
The argument supplies a geopolitical instance of religion poisoning civic life by connecting sectarian faith, theocratic government, social collapse, and violence against civilians.
The audience member's question about whether Hitchens and Olasky support the Iraq war because of ideological vanity or religious commonality.
Hitchens characterizes faith-based factions as degrading Iraqi civilization and presents continued defense of secular government against jihadist rule as a major moral undertaking.
Pascal's wager encourages self-interested professions rather than honest belief, making sincere nonbelief more moral, candid, and courageous than calculated piety.
The response attacks a prominent pragmatic defense of belief and turns the motion toward moral character by contrasting truthful doubt with opportunistic religious profession.
The final audience member's request that Hitchens answer Pascal's wager as a reason to adopt belief before death.
Hitchens rejects the wager as manipulative inducement, cites insufficient evidence as a defense of unbelief, and argues that an honest doubter is morally preferable to a strategic professed believer.
